verse.text: Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother,

to the assembly of God that is in Corinth, to those made holy in Christ Jesus, called to be holy ones, together with all those who in every place call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours:
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering of citizens, and in the Greek Old Testament it names Israel assembled before God. ‘Church’ is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. ‘Assembly’ is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one Greek word, though it can wrongly sound like a one-off meeting.

Paul uses this term for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God’s people’. The preceding ‘made holy’ is the related verb.

The Greek says only ‘theirs and ours’, which could go with ‘Lord’ (he is Lord of believers everywhere as well as of Paul and the Corinthians) or with ‘place’ (‘in every place, theirs and ours’). Most translations and commentators take it with ‘Lord’, as here, but the word order allows the other reading.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I always thank my God for you because of the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus,
for in everything you were made rich in him, in all speech and all knowledge,
just as the testimony about Christ was established among you,
so that you are not lacking in any gift as you eagerly await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.
He will also establish you to the end, beyond reproach on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
God is faithful, and through him you were called into partnership with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
verse.note: The word means sharing something in common and was used of business partnerships, marriage and other joint ventures. ‘Fellowship’ is the traditional rendering but now tends to suggest friendly socialising. The Greek phrase could also be read as ‘sharing in his Son’, that is, participation in Christ and not only association with him; the two readings are not far apart.

verse.text: Now I appeal to you, brothers and sisters, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be knit together in the same mind and the same judgment.
For it has been made clear to me about you, my brothers and sisters, by Chloe’s people, that there are quarrels among you.

note.traditional: those of the household of Chloe

verse.note: The Greek says simply ‘those of Chloe’, meaning members of her household, most likely slaves, freed persons or business agents who travelled between Corinth and Ephesus, where Paul was writing. Nothing else is known about Chloe, including whether she lived in Corinth or was herself a believer.

verse.text: What I mean is this: each of you is saying, “I belong to Paul,” “I belong to Apollos,” “I belong to Cephas,” “I belong to Christ.”
verse.note: Cephas is the Aramaic name, meaning ‘rock’, of the apostle better known by its Greek equivalent, Peter. Paul usually calls him Cephas. Whether Peter had actually visited Corinth or was simply revered there by some is not known.

verse.text: Has Christ been divided up? Paul was not crucified for you, was he? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?
I am thankful that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,
verse.note: Some of the earliest manuscripts read simply ‘I give thanks’, which is the text translated here. Most manuscripts add ‘to God’, and many English versions follow them. The sense is hardly affected.

verse.text: so that no one can say that you were baptized into my name.
I did also baptize the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.
For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the good news, and not with wisdom of words, so that the cross of Christ would not be made empty.
verse.note: Trained public speaking was highly prized in Greek cities such as Corinth, and a speaker’s skill was taken as a sign of his wisdom and standing. Paul’s phrase, literally ‘wisdom of word’, refers to that kind of polished rhetoric or clever argument. The same Greek term is picked up in the next verse as ‘the word of the cross’, so ‘word’ is kept in both places.

verse.text: For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the intelligence of the intelligent I will set aside.”

note.term: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 29:14, in a form close to the ancient Greek translation. In Isaiah the words are God’s judgment on the political advisers of Judah who trusted their own shrewdness.

verse.text: Where is the wise person? Where is the scholar? Where is the debater of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of the world foolish?
verse.note: In Jewish settings this word means a trained expert in the Scriptures and the Law, not a copyist, which is what ‘scribe’ suggests in English today. Most interpreters think Paul is setting the Jewish expert beside the Greek sage and the public debater, with echoes of Isaiah 19:12 and 33:18. In a Greek city the same word could also mean a civic secretary, but that sense is unlikely here.

verse.text: For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not come to know God through wisdom, God was pleased, through the foolishness of the proclamation, to save those who believe.
For Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom,
but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,
verse.note: The Greek word means ‘nations’ or ‘peoples’, and in the plural was the standard Jewish term for all peoples other than Israel; English versions render the one word as ‘Gentiles’ or ‘nations’ according to context. Here Paul uses it interchangeably with ‘Greeks’ in verses 22 and 24.

verse.text: but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
For the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings.
Look at your own calling, brothers and sisters: not many were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were well-born.
But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong,
and God chose the low-born things of the world and the despised, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are,
so that no flesh may boast before God.
verse.note: ‘All flesh’ is a Hebrew way of saying ‘every human being’, with an overtone of human frailty before God; the idiom is kept here. The same Greek word lies behind ‘by human standards’ in verse 26, which is literally ‘according to the flesh’, so Paul’s argument begins and ends with merely human measures of worth.

verse.text: It is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and holiness and redemption,
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and God’s action to set things right. ‘Righteousness’ is kept because ‘justice’ would suggest punishment to many modern readers, though some scholars prefer ‘justice’.

verse.text: so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

note.term: Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.

verse.note: This is a condensed form of Jeremiah 9:24 (9:23 in the Greek version), not a word-for-word citation; the surrounding verses in Jeremiah warn the wise, the strong and the rich not to boast, which matches verses 26 to 28 here. In Jeremiah ‘the Lord’ is Israel’s God. Whether Paul means God or Christ by ‘the Lord’ here is debated.

verse.text: And when I came to you, brothers and sisters, I did not come with superiority of speech or of wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony of God.
verse.note: The Greek masculine plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group, and Paul is writing to the whole congregation, women included. Many recent translations render it this way; others keep “brothers” and leave the inclusion to be understood.

note.traditional: the testimony of God / the mystery of God

verse.note: Early manuscripts are divided here between “testimony” (martyrion) and “mystery” (mystērion), two words that differ by only a few letters. The SBLGNT, translated here, prints “testimony”; other critical editions print “mystery”, and English versions differ accordingly. Either reading suits the context, and the question is open.

verse.text: For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
And I was with you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling,
and my speech and my proclamation came not with the persuasiveness of wisdom but with a demonstration of the Spirit and of power,
verse.note: This phrase has come down in many slightly different forms. The most familiar is “persuasive words of wisdom”, to which some manuscripts add “human”. The SBLGNT adopts a shorter form, “persuasion of wisdom”. The sense is the same in every form: Paul did not rely on the rhetorical technique that Corinthians admired.

verse.text: so that your faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God.
Yet we do speak wisdom among the mature, though a wisdom not of this age nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing.

note.traditional: the princes of this world / the rulers of this age

verse.note: The word ordinarily means human rulers, and on that reading Paul means the authorities who had Jesus crucified (verse 8). Many interpreters think he means, or also means, the spiritual powers standing behind those authorities, since he uses similar language for such powers elsewhere. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

verse.text: Rather, we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden, which God determined in advance, before the ages, for our glory.
verse.note: In Paul, as in Jewish writings in Greek such as Daniel, this word does not mean a puzzle. It means a secret purpose of God that can be known only because God discloses it. “In a mystery” may describe how the wisdom is spoken or the form in which the wisdom exists; the Greek allows either.

The verb means to decide or mark out beforehand. Most translations use “predestined” or “decreed”. “Predestined” now carries the weight of later doctrinal debates about the fate of individuals, whereas here what God determined is the wisdom itself, that is, the plan centred on the crucified Christ.

verse.text: None of the rulers of this age has known it, for if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
But as it is written: “What eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and what has not arisen in the human heart, all that God has prepared for those who love him.”
verse.note: No passage of the Jewish Scriptures matches this quotation word for word. The closest is Isaiah 64:4, and the phrase about the heart resembles Isaiah 65:17; Paul may be quoting freely or combining texts. “Arisen in the heart” is a Semitic way of saying that a thought has occurred to someone.

verse.text: For to us God has revealed them through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
verse.note: Manuscripts divide between “for” and “but” at the start of this verse. The SBLGNT prints “for”, which makes the verse explain how what was prepared came to be known. With “but”, the verse contrasts “us” with the rulers who did not know.

verse.text: For who among people knows the things of a person except the person’s spirit that is within? So too, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.
Now we have received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may know the things freely given to us by God.
And we speak of these things not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people.

note.term: interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people

verse.note: The Greek is compressed, and both the verb and the word “spiritual” in the dative are ambiguous. The verb can mean interpret (its sense in the Greek Old Testament, of dreams), compare, or combine, and the dative can be “to spiritual people” or “with spiritual words”. The chief alternative is therefore “fitting spiritual things to spiritual words”. The rendering here follows the Septuagint sense and the contrast of persons in verses 14–15, but the matter is disputed.

verse.text: But a natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for to such a person they are foolishness; nor can that person know them, because they are examined spiritually.
verse.note: The adjective comes from the word for the life or soul that every living person has, and Paul sets it against “spiritual”, meaning of God’s Spirit. A “natural” person is someone living with ordinary human resources alone, without the Spirit. It is not a comment on intelligence or character. Some translations paraphrase as “unspiritual” or “the person without the Spirit”.

Paul uses the same verb three times in verses 14–15, and most translations vary it, with “discerned” in verse 14 and “judges” in verse 15. The word means to examine or investigate, often in a judicial hearing, and Paul uses it again of the Corinthians’ scrutiny of him in 4:3–4. One English word is kept here so that the repetition can be heard.

verse.text: The spiritual person examines everything, yet that person is examined by no one.
For “who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 40:13 in its Greek form, where “the Lord” is Israel’s God and the expected answer is “no one”. The Hebrew has “spirit” where the Greek version has “mind”, which suits Paul’s argument about the Spirit. He then answers the question with the claim that “we have the mind of Christ”.

verse.text: And I, brothers and sisters, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as people of flesh, as infants in Christ.
verse.note: Paul uses two related adjectives: one in verse 1 that normally means 'made of flesh', and one in verse 3 that means 'characterised by flesh'. They are rendered 'people of flesh' and 'fleshly' to keep them distinct. 'Carnal' now suggests sexual sin, which is not the point here; other versions use 'worldly' or 'unspiritual'. Whether Paul intends a real difference between the two words is debated.

verse.text: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it. In fact, you are still not able even now,
for you are still fleshly. For where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly and living in a merely human way?

note.term: living in a merely human way

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'walking according to a human being'. 'Walk' is a Semitic idiom for how one conducts one's life, and Greek-speaking Jews used it that way. 'Merely' is supplied to bring out the contrast with life shaped by the Spirit, as it is in verse 4.

verse.text: For when someone says, “I belong to Paul,” and another, “I belong to Apollos,” are you not merely human?
What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, as the Lord assigned to each.
I planted, Apollos watered, but God was making it grow.
So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God, who makes it grow.
The one who plants and the one who waters are one, and each will receive his own wages according to his own labor.
verse.note: The word is the ordinary term for a worker's pay, and it fits the picture of field hands and builders that runs through the passage. Many translations use 'wages' here and 'reward' in verse 14; the same word is kept in both places so that the link stays visible.

verse.text: For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building.
verse.note: The Greek can mean 'people who work alongside God' or 'fellow workers who belong to God', that is, Paul and Apollos as colleagues in God's service. The second fits the surrounding argument, which plays down the workers and stresses that everything is God's, but both readings have scholarly support. The English is left open to either.

verse.text: According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building on it. But each one must take care how he builds on it.
verse.note: The adjective is the same word translated 'wise' in verses 18–20. It was the normal term for a skilled craftsman, and the Greek version of Isaiah 3:3 has the same phrase. A Greek reader would hear the echo of the letter's argument about wisdom, which the English 'skilled' does not carry. The 'master builder' was the person who directed a building project, not a designer in the modern sense of 'architect'.

verse.text: For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw,
each one’s work will become visible, for the Day will make it clear, because it is revealed in fire, and the fire itself will test what kind of work each one’s is.
verse.note: This is the 'day of the Lord' of the prophets, the day of God's judgment, which Paul elsewhere calls the day of the Lord Jesus Christ (1:8). The prophets often link fire with that day. The capital letter is an English convention to mark this; the Greek has simply 'the day'.

note.traditional: it shall be revealed by fire

verse.note: The subject of 'is revealed' is not stated. Most interpreters take it to be the Day, which arrives with fire; others take it to be each person's work, which the fire exposes. The English 'it' leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: If the work that anyone has built on it remains, he will receive wages.
If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
verse.note: The picture is of someone who escapes through the flames of a burning building with nothing but his life. The fire in this passage tests the quality of work built on the foundation, and the people in view are those who build up the community. The verse later became important in debates about purgatory, but most modern scholars of all traditions read it as an image of narrow escape, not a description of purifying punishment.

verse.text: Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God lives in you?

note.traditional: ye are the temple of God

verse.note: 'You' is plural throughout verses 16–17 and 'temple' is singular: the community as a whole is the temple, continuing the building image of verses 9–15. The word used is the one for the sanctuary proper, the place where the deity dwells, not for the wider temple precincts. Paul applies the image to the individual body later, in 6:19.

verse.text: If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person; for God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are.
verse.note: Paul uses the same verb twice, side by side: whoever does this to God's temple, God will do it to him. The verb can mean 'ruin', 'corrupt' or 'destroy'. Some older versions translate the first as 'defile' and the second as 'destroy', which hides the deliberate repetition. 'Destroy' is used for both, though the first may carry the nuance of damaging or corrupting the community.

verse.text: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool so that he may become wise.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. For it is written: “He catches the wise in their own cunning,”

note.term: “He catches the wise in their own cunning,”
note.traditional: He taketh the wise in their own craftiness

verse.note: The quotation is from Job 5:13, from a speech of Eliphaz. Paul's wording differs from the standard Greek version of Job and is closer to the Hebrew. In Greek it is not a full sentence but a descriptive phrase, 'the one who catches the wise'.

verse.text: and again: “The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.”
verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 94:11 (93:11 in the Greek numbering). The psalm speaks of the thoughts 'of people'; Paul's quotation has 'of the wise', which applies the line directly to his argument about human wisdom.

verse.text: So let no one boast in human beings. For all things are yours,
whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours,
and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
This is how a person should regard us: as Christ's assistants and stewards of God's secrets.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a subordinate who carries out someone else's instructions: an aide, attendant or junior official. It is not Paul's usual word for a servant or a slave, and 'assistants' keeps that distinction visible. Most modern translations have 'servants'.

In the Greek Scriptures and in Paul the word means something God has kept hidden and now discloses, not a puzzle or something beyond understanding, which is what 'mystery' suggests today. Most translations keep 'mysteries', and some scholars defend it as an established technical term.

A steward was the manager of a household or estate, often himself a slave, who ran the owner's affairs and answered to the owner alone. That is the point of verses 2 to 5: a steward is assessed by his master, not by the rest of the household.

verse.text: Now in this matter what is required of stewards is that one be found faithful.
But to me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you or by any human court; in fact, I do not even examine myself.
verse.note: The Greek says literally 'a human day', meaning a day of judgment set by human beings. The phrase is coined to contrast with 'the Day' of the Lord's judgment mentioned in 3:13. English translations generally paraphrase it as a human court or human judgment.

verse.text: For I am aware of nothing against myself, but I am not vindicated by that; the one who examines me is the Lord.
verse.note: The verb belongs to the word-family English splits between 'righteous' and 'just', and is traditionally rendered 'justify'. Here the setting is a judicial examination, and the meaning is to be declared in the right. Several modern versions accordingly have 'acquitted' or 'innocent' at this verse.

verse.text: So do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes. He will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and make plain the intentions of hearts, and then each one's praise will come from God.

Now, brothers and sisters, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that from us you may learn the saying “Not beyond what is written,” so that none of you is puffed up in favor of the one against the other.
verse.note: The verb normally means to change the form or appearance of something, and its exact sense here is debated. The usual view is that Paul has cast his argument in terms of himself and Apollos as an illustration, perhaps to avoid naming those in Corinth whom it really concerns. Others take it to mean simply that he has spoken figuratively, through the images of gardeners, builders and stewards.

The Greek is a terse phrase with no verb, introduced as if it were a known saying. Most interpreters take 'what is written' to mean Scripture, perhaps the passages Paul has quoted in chapters 1 to 3. Its origin and exact force are uncertain, and a few scholars have suspected that the text is damaged at this point.

verse.text: For who marks you out as different? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?
Already you have had your fill! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And I wish you really had become kings, so that we too might be kings with you!
For it seems to me that God has put us apostles on show last of all, like men condemned to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, both to angels and to people.
verse.note: The picture is drawn from public shows in the arena or theater, or possibly from a victory procession. Condemned prisoners were brought on at the end to be killed before the crowd. Paul pictures the apostles in that last place, with the whole universe as the audience.

verse.text: We are fools because of Christ, but you are sensible in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored.
To this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are knocked about, we have no home,
and we toil, working with our own hands. When insulted, we bless; when persecuted, we endure;
when slandered, we answer kindly. We have become like the scum of the world, the scrapings of everything, right up to now.
verse.note: This word and the one rendered 'scrapings' both refer to the dirt removed when something is scoured or wiped clean. Both were also used as insults for worthless people. Some scholars think they also allude to human scapegoats sacrificed to purify a city, which would make the apostles victims on behalf of others, but whether Paul intends that is disputed.

verse.text: I am not writing these things to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.
For though you may have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus, through the good news, it was I who fathered you.
verse.note: The word refers to the household slave who escorted a boy to school and supervised his conduct until he came of age. He was a minder and disciplinarian, not a teacher. The contrast is between any number of hired supervisors and the one father.

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, including imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has become a purely religious term or a book title. Many modern translations alternate between the two renderings.

verse.text: So I urge you: become imitators of me.
For this reason I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. He will remind you of my ways in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every assembly.
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Greek Scriptures' term for Israel assembled. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering, and 'assembly' should be understood here as a standing community, not a single meeting.

verse.text: But some have become puffed up, as though I were not coming to you.
But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up but their power,
for the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power.
What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?
verse.note: 'Meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek does not; the word describes someone who is not harsh or self-assertive. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the mainstream modern rendering.

verse.text: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and sexual immorality of a kind not found even among the Gentiles: a man has his father’s wife.
verse.note: The older English rendering “fornication” now suggests only sex between unmarried people. In Jewish Greek of the period the word covered any sexual relationship outside what the law permitted, including incest, as here. Most modern translations make the same choice.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations” and in the plural regularly refers to the non-Jewish peoples; elsewhere in this translation the same word appears as “nations.” Most of the Corinthian believers were themselves non-Jews by birth, so Paul is using the word for those outside the community of faith.

The phrase echoes the wording of Leviticus 18:8 and means a stepmother rather than the man's own mother. The verb “has” points to an ongoing relationship, whether marriage or cohabitation, not a single act. Roman law also forbade such unions, which is the point of saying that even the Gentiles do not tolerate it.

verse.text: And you are puffed up! Should you not rather have mourned, so that the one who did this deed would be removed from among you?
For I, absent in body but present in spirit, have already passed judgment, as though I were present, on the one who has done such a thing:
in the name of our Lord Jesus, when you are gathered together, and my spirit with you, with the power of our Lord Jesus,

note.term: in the name of our Lord Jesus
note.traditional: in the name of our Lord Jesus

verse.note: The Greek of verses 3–5 is one long sentence, and it is unclear what this phrase attaches to. It may go with “I have passed judgment,” with “when you are gathered together,” or with “hand such a man over.” The translation keeps the Greek order and leaves the connection open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: you are to hand such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.
verse.note: This is disputed. Some take “flesh” as the man's body, so that exclusion from the community exposes him to physical suffering or even death. Others take it as his sinful orientation, which the discipline is meant to break. The Greek says “the flesh” and “the spirit” without “his,” and the translation leaves it so.

note.traditional: the day of the Lord Jesus

verse.note: Some manuscripts read “the day of the Lord Jesus” or “the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The shorter reading is found in early witnesses and is the one followed here; scribes were more likely to expand the title than to shorten it.

verse.text: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole batch of dough?
verse.note: Leaven was not packaged yeast but a lump of fermented dough kept back from an earlier batch and worked into the next one. Before Passover, Jewish households cleared every trace of it from the house and ate unleavened bread for seven days (Exodus 12:15–20). Paul's image in verses 6–8 depends on that custom.

verse.text: Clean out the old leaven so that you may be a new batch, just as you are in fact unleavened. For indeed Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
verse.note: The Greek has simply “our Passover.” In the Septuagint and in Jewish usage, “to sacrifice the Passover” meant to slaughter the lamb eaten at the festival, so the word here refers to the animal. Most modern translations add “lamb” for that reason.

verse.text: So let us keep the festival, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—
verse.note: Paul refers to an earlier letter to Corinth, written before 1 Corinthians, which has not survived. The Corinthians had apparently taken its instruction to mean avoiding immoral people in general, and he now clarifies it.

verse.text: not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and robbers, or idolaters, since then you would have to go out of the world.

But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone called a brother if he is sexually immoral or greedy, or an idolater, or abusive, or a drunkard, or a robber—not even to eat with such a person.

note.traditional: But now I have written / But now I am writing

verse.note: The verb is the same past-tense form as “I wrote” in verse 9. It can be an epistolary past referring to the present letter (“now I am writing”), as most translations take it. Or “now” can be logical, not temporal: “but in fact what I wrote was….” On the second reading Paul is explaining what the earlier letter meant, not adding a new instruction.

The word describes someone who insults and verbally abuses others, usually to their face. “Slanderer,” found in some translations, suggests spreading false reports behind someone's back, which is a different word in Greek.

verse.text: For what business of mine is it to judge those outside? Is it not those inside whom you judge,
while God judges those outside? “Remove the wicked person from among yourselves.”

note.term: Remove the wicked person from among yourselves.
note.traditional: Put away from among yourselves that wicked person

verse.note: Paul closes with a command that recurs in Deuteronomy (for example 17:7; 22:21, 24), quoted in the wording of the Greek translation with the verb changed to the plural. In Deuteronomy the formula concludes rulings on offences, including sexual ones, that required removing the offender from Israel. Paul gives no introductory formula, but his readers who knew the Scriptures would have recognised it.

verse.text: Does any one of you who has a dispute with another dare to go to court before the unjust and not before the holy ones?
verse.note: The word describes people who are not in the right. Here it labels outsiders to the community (the 'unbelievers' of v. 6) and does not accuse particular judges of corruption, though some scholars think Paul also has in mind the bias of civil courts toward the wealthy. 'Unjust' is used so that the reader can hear the thread Paul runs through the passage: the same Greek root returns in 'treated unjustly' (v. 7), 'act unjustly' (v. 8), 'the unjust' (v. 9) and 'justified' (v. 11).

Paul uses this term for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'. The related verb in v. 11, traditionally 'sanctified', is rendered 'made holy' so that the connection stays visible.

verse.text: Or do you not know that the holy ones will judge the world? And if the world is judged by you, are you unfit to try the smallest cases?
verse.note: The Greek noun can mean either a court that hears a case or the case itself. The phrase could therefore be 'unworthy to sit on the lowest courts'. 'Cases' is chosen because the same word in v. 4 is something the Corinthians 'have'. The point is the same on either reading.

verse.text: Do you not know that we will judge angels, to say nothing of everyday matters?
So if you have cases over everyday matters, do you seat as judges those who count for nothing in the assembly?
verse.note: The Greek verb form can be a question, a statement or a command. Read as a question, as here, 'those who count for nothing in the assembly' are outside judges, who have no standing in the community. Read as a command (so the King James Version), Paul says with irony that even the least regarded members of the community are fit to settle such trivial matters. Most recent translations take it as a question.

A first-century hearer knew this word as the term for a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution, which the word did not mean. 'Church' is nonetheless the near-universal rendering, and readers should understand the same community is meant.

verse.text: I say this to shame you. Is it really so, that there is not one wise person among you who will be able to decide between one brother and another,
but brother goes to court against brother, and this before unbelievers?
In fact, it is already a complete defeat for you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why not rather be treated unjustly? Why not rather be defrauded?
But you yourselves act unjustly and defraud, and this to brothers!

Or do you not know that the unjust will not inherit God’s kingdom? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who take the passive role in sex with males, nor men who lie with males,
verse.note: This word belongs to a family Paul uses throughout the chapter: 'sexual immorality' (vv. 13, 18), 'commits sexual immorality' (v. 18) and 'prostitute' (vv. 15–16) all share its root. The family began with prostitution. In Jewish Greek it had widened to cover any sexual relations outside marriage.

note.term: men who take the passive role in sex with males

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'soft ones'. Applied to men, it was a term of contempt for unmanliness and was commonly used of males who took the receptive role in sex with other males. Its position between 'adulterers' and the next term makes that narrower sense the likely one here, and this is the view of the standard lexicons. Some scholars argue for a broader meaning (self-indulgent, lacking self-control), and some translations render 'male prostitutes' or merge it with the following word. The rendering is disputed.

note.traditional: homosexuals; sodomites; abusers of themselves with mankind

verse.note: This word is not found before Paul. It joins 'male' and 'bed' (a common expression for intercourse), and appears to be built from the Greek of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, where the two words stand side by side. Most scholars take it to mean men who have sex with males, and, paired with the preceding term, the active partner. Some argue it referred more narrowly to pederasty or sexual exploitation. 'Homosexuals' is avoided because it names an orientation, a modern category, where the Greek names an act.

verse.text: nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor the verbally abusive, nor robbers will inherit the kingdom of God.
And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, but you were made holy, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and in the Spirit of our God.
“Everything is permitted me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permitted me,” but I will not be mastered by anything.

note.traditional: All things are lawful unto me

verse.note: Most scholars think Paul is here quoting a slogan current among some in Corinth, perhaps a distortion of his own teaching on freedom, and then qualifying it. The quotation marks reflect that judgment; the Greek has none. The slogan returns in 10:23.

verse.text: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will do away with both the one and the other.” But the body is not for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.

note.term: and God will do away with both the one and the other

verse.note: It is uncertain where the Corinthian slogan ends. Some translations close the quotation after 'food' and take this clause as Paul's own comment. It is included in the slogan here because Paul's reply matches it point for point: body for the Lord, the Lord for the body, and God will raise the body, not do away with it. On that reading the Corinthians argued that what is done with a perishable body does not matter, and Paul denies it.

verse.text: And God both raised the Lord and will raise us up through his power.
Do you not know that your bodies are limbs of Christ? Shall I then take the limbs of Christ and make them limbs of a prostitute? Absolutely not!
verse.note: The Greek word means a limb or part of a body. 'Members' once meant the same, but now suggests belonging to a group, which hides how physical the image is. Paul's argument is that the believer's body is part of Christ's body, and so cannot be made part of a prostitute's. Most translations keep 'members'.

verse.text: Or do you not know that whoever is joined to a prostitute is one body with her? For “The two,” it says, “will become one flesh.”
But whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him.
Flee sexual immorality. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but whoever commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.
Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? And you are not your own,
for you were bought at a price. So glorify God in your body.
verse.note: This is the language of the marketplace, and a first-century reader would have heard in it the purchase of a slave, who then belongs to the buyer. That is why Paul can say 'you are not your own'. He does not say here what the price was or to whom it was paid.

verse.text: Now concerning the things you wrote about: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.”

note.term: It is good for a man not to touch a woman
note.traditional: It is good for a man not to touch a woman (read as Paul's own statement)

verse.note: The Greek has no quotation marks, and older translations read this as Paul's own view. Most recent scholars take it as a line from the Corinthians' letter that Paul quotes and then qualifies in verses 2–5, and the text is punctuated that way here; the other reading remains possible. 'Touch a woman' was an established euphemism for sexual intercourse, not for marriage or for physical contact in general.

verse.text: But because of the cases of sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman should have her own husband.
The husband should give his wife what is owed her, and likewise the wife her husband.
The wife does not have authority over her own body; her husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body; his wife does.

Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer and then be together again, so that Satan does not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
I say this as a concession, not as a command.
I wish that everyone were as I myself am. But each person has their own gift from God, one of this kind and another of that.
To the unmarried and the widows I say: it is good for them if they remain as I am.
But if they are not exercising self-control, they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn.

note.traditional: to burn (KJV); to burn with passion (most modern versions)

verse.note: The Greek says only 'to burn'. Most interpreters understand burning with sexual desire, and many translations add 'with passion'. A minority take it as burning in judgment, so the bare verb is kept.

verse.text: To the married I give this instruction—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not separate from her husband;
verse.note: Greek and Roman law had no category of separation short of divorce: a spouse who left the marriage had ended it, and 'separate' was an ordinary word for divorcing. 'Not I, but the Lord' points to Jesus' own teaching against divorce, preserved in the Gospels (for example Mark 10:2–12). In verse 12 Paul marks where he goes beyond what that teaching addressed.

verse.text: but if she does separate, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband should not divorce his wife.
To the rest I say—I, not the Lord—if any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her.
And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce her husband.
For the unbelieving husband has been made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife has been made holy through the brother. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is they are holy.
verse.note: The verb is from the same root as the 'holy' said of the children at the end of the verse, and 'made holy' keeps that link visible where 'sanctified' hides it. Paul does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved, since verse 16 treats that as still open. The usual view is that the marriage and its children fall within the sphere of God's people rather than defiling the believer, though exactly what Paul means is debated.

verse.text: But if the unbeliever separates, let him separate. The brother or the sister is not enslaved in such cases; God has called us to peace.

note.traditional: called us (KJV, NASB); called you (ESV, NIV, NRSV)

verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between 'us' and 'you', which differ by one letter in Greek and were pronounced alike. SBLGNT reads 'us'; several other critical editions and many modern translations read 'you'. The sense is hardly affected.

verse.text: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
Only, as the Lord has apportioned to each, as God has called each, so let each one walk. And this is what I direct in all the assemblies.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word appears as one English word.

verse.text: Was anyone called when already circumcised? He should not undo his circumcision. Has anyone been called while uncircumcised? He should not be circumcised.

note.traditional: become uncircumcised; remove the marks of circumcision

verse.note: The verb refers to a known procedure for stretching or restoring the foreskin. Some Jewish men underwent it to avoid ridicule in the Greek gymnasium and baths, where men exercised and bathed naked. 1 Maccabees 1:15 mentions the practice.

verse.text: Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing; what counts is keeping God’s commandments.
Each person should remain in the calling in which they were called.
Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you. But if you are in fact able to become free, rather take the opportunity.

note.traditional: use it rather (KJV); avail yourself of the opportunity

verse.note: The Greek says only 'rather make use', with no object. Most modern translators and commentators supply 'the chance of freedom', as here. A substantial minority, ancient and modern, supply 'your slavery': 'even if you can become free, make use of your present condition instead'. The grammar permits both; the tense of the verb and the 'but' that opens the clause are usually thought to favour the first.

verse.text: For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freed person; likewise the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave.
You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of people.
Brothers and sisters, in whatever condition each was called, in that let each remain with God.
Now concerning the virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is faithful.
I think, then, that this is good because of the present distress: that it is good for a person to stay as they are.
verse.note: The participle can mean 'present' or 'impending', and the noun covers necessity, hardship and crisis. Some think Paul means a local hardship at Corinth, such as a food shortage. Others think he means the pressures of the last days, which verses 29–31 have in view. The rendering leaves this open.

verse.text: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife.
But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if the virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such people will have affliction in the flesh, and I am trying to spare you.
What I mean, brothers and sisters, is this: the time has been cut short. From now on, even those who have wives should be as though they had none,
those who weep as though they were not weeping, those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, those who buy as though they did not own,
and those who make use of the world as though they were not making full use of it. For the form of this world is passing away.
I want you to be free of concern. The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord;
but the married man is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife,

and he is divided. The unmarried woman, and the virgin, is concerned with the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy both in body and in spirit; but the married woman is concerned with the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

note.traditional: There is difference also between a wife and a virgin (KJV)

verse.note: The manuscripts vary considerably in wording and punctuation at this point. The text followed here attaches 'and he is divided' to the married man of verse 33 and begins a new sentence about the unmarried woman and the virgin. The reading behind the KJV instead makes 'divided' the start of a statement that wife and virgin differ. Most modern editions and translations agree with the reading adopted here.

verse.text: I say this for your own benefit, not to throw a noose around you, but for the sake of what is proper and of undistracted devotion to the Lord.
But if anyone thinks he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, if she is passing her prime and so it ought to be, let him do what he wishes; he is not sinning. Let them marry.

note.traditional: his virgin (KJV); his virgin daughter (NASB); his betrothed (ESV), his fiancée (NRSV)

verse.note: Verses 36–38 are among the most disputed in Paul. The older view is that a father is deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage, and the verb in verse 38 normally means 'give in marriage'. Most recent scholars think an engaged man is deciding whether to marry his fiancée, which suits 'let them marry' here, and they argue that the verb in verse 38 could by this period also mean simply 'marry'. The translation follows the second view but keeps Paul's own word 'virgin', as in verse 25.

note.term: if she is passing her prime
note.traditional: if she pass the flower of her age (KJV); if his passions are strong (ESV, NRSV)

verse.note: The adjective is rare. Its attested uses and related words refer to being past the bloom of youth, which for a woman meant past the usual age for marriage; that sense is followed here. Many modern translations instead take the man as the subject and render 'if his passions are strong', which is also possible and fits the stress on self-mastery in verse 37.

verse.text: But the one who stands firm in his heart, under no compulsion but having authority over his own will, and has decided this in his own heart, to keep his virgin as she is, will do well.
So then, the one who marries his virgin does well, and the one who does not marry will do better.
A wife is bound for as long as her husband lives. But if her husband falls asleep, she is free to be married to whomever she wishes, only in the Lord.
verse.note: The Greek verb is literally 'fall asleep', a common euphemism for dying which Paul uses repeatedly of believers (for example in chapter 15). Most translations render it 'dies' here. The image is kept so that the same expression reads the same way throughout the letter.

verse.text: But she is more blessed if she remains as she is, in my judgment; and I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
Now about food sacrificed to idols: we know that “we all have knowledge.” Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
verse.note: In a city like Corinth, much of the meat available came from animals offered in temples. Part was burned, part went to the priests, and the rest was eaten at temple meals or sold in the market. The Greek term is a Jewish and Christian one; a pagan would have said simply “sacred offering.” The question put to Paul is whether believers may eat such food.

note.traditional: we know that we all have knowledge

verse.note: Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks. Most scholars think Paul is here quoting a slogan from the Corinthians' letter to him and then qualifying it. The same is widely held for the two statements quoted in verse 4, and some extend it to verse 8. The words can also be read as Paul's own, which he then limits.

verse.text: If anyone thinks they have come to know something, they do not yet know as they ought to know.
But if anyone loves God, that person is known by him.

note.term: that person is known by him
note.traditional: the same is known of him

verse.note: A few early witnesses, including the oldest papyrus copy of Paul's letters, have a shorter text: “if anyone loves, that person is known.” Most manuscripts and most editors have the longer reading translated here. On either reading the point is that being known by God matters more than what one knows.

verse.text: So then, about eating food sacrificed to idols: we know that “an idol is nothing in the world” and that “there is no God but one.”

note.term: “an idol is nothing in the world”
note.traditional: an idol is nothing in the world

verse.note: The Greek can also be read “there is no idol in the world,” meaning that no idol has real existence. That reading makes a closer parallel with “there is no God but one.” Many recent translations follow it. Either way the claim is that the gods the images represent are not real gods.

verse.text: For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—
yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things come and through whom we exist.
verse.note: The sentence has no verbs in Greek and has the rhythm of a confession. Its wording echoes Israel's daily declaration, “The Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). “God” is applied to the Father and “Lord” to Jesus Christ. Many scholars take this as Paul including Jesus within Israel's confession of the one God, though how much to draw from it is debated.

verse.text: But this knowledge is not in everyone. Some, from being used to idols until now, eat this food as food sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.

note.term: from being used to idols until now

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “custom” or “habit” (synētheia). The later majority reads “conscience” (syneidēsis), which the King James Version follows; it is probably a slip caused by the same word later in the verse. Modern editions and translations follow the earlier reading.

verse.text: But food will not bring us near to God; for we are no better off if we eat, and no worse off if we do not.
verse.note: The verb means to present or place someone before another. Here it may mean winning God's favour (“commend”) or, in a courtroom sense, bringing us before God for judgment. In either case the point is that eating or not eating does not affect one's standing with God. Some scholars think this sentence is another Corinthian slogan.

verse.text: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.
For if someone sees you, the one with knowledge, reclining at table in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience, weak as he is, be built up to eat food sacrificed to idols?

note.term: reclining at table in an idol’s temple
note.traditional: sit at meat in the idol's temple

verse.note: Temples had dining rooms where people reclined for meals, as was the custom at formal dinners. Such meals marked family occasions, club gatherings and civic events, so declining them carried a social cost. Paul's example is of a believer seen at one of these dinners.

Most translations have “emboldened” or “encouraged.” The Greek verb is the same one used in verse 1, “love builds up.” Paul's repetition is ironic: the knowing person's example “builds up” the weak one into doing what will destroy him. The rendering keeps the echo.

verse.text: For the one who is weak is being destroyed by your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died.
verse.note: “Brother” was the ordinary term among early believers for a fellow member of the community, and it included women as well as men. The singular is kept here and in verse 13 because Paul is picturing one individual.

verse.text: And so, by sinning against your brothers and striking their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
verse.note: The verb ordinarily means to hit or beat someone. “Wounding” is the traditional rendering and describes the result. “Striking” keeps the plain sense of the word: the act is pictured as a blow against a conscience that cannot withstand it.

verse.text: Therefore, if food causes my brother to fall, I will never eat meat again, so that I may not cause my brother to fall.
Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord?
If to others I am not an apostle, to you at least I am; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
This is my defense to those who are examining me.
Do we not have the right to eat and drink?
Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as the other apostles do, and the Lord’s brothers, and Cephas?
verse.note: The Greek is literally “a sister, a wife”, where “sister” means a fellow believer, as “brother” does throughout the letter. The second word can mean either “woman” or “wife”, and some early interpreters took the phrase to mean a Christian woman who travelled as an assistant. Nearly all modern scholars read it as a wife who is a believer, supported at the churches’ expense along with her husband.

verse.text: Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working?
Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Who shepherds a flock and does not have some of the flock’s milk?
Am I saying this from a merely human standpoint, or does the law not say the same?
For in the law of Moses it is written: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.” Is it the oxen God cares about,

note.term: You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.

verse.note: The quotation is Deuteronomy 25:4. Grain was threshed by driving oxen over the cut stalks, and the law let the animal eat as it worked. Paul argues from the lesser case to the greater, a common form of reasoning among Jewish interpreters of the time.

verse.text: or is he surely speaking for our sake? Yes, it was written for our sake, because the plowman ought to plow in hope, and the thresher to thresh in hope of having a share.
verse.note: The Greek adverb can mean “certainly” or “entirely”. On the second reading Paul would be saying the law was written wholly for people and not for oxen at all. On the reading adopted here he says only that it undoubtedly applies to human workers as well.

verse.text: If we sowed spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap material things from you?

If others share this right over you, do we not even more? But we did not make use of this right. Instead we put up with everything, so as not to put any obstacle in the way of the good news of Christ.
verse.note: “Gospel” has become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations, and that is what Paul’s readers heard. Many modern translations already alternate between “gospel” and “good news”.

verse.text: Do you not know that those who work in the temple service eat what comes from the temple, and those who attend at the altar share in what is offered on the altar?
In the same way the Lord also directed that those who proclaim the good news should live from the good news.
verse.note: Paul appeals to an instruction of Jesus. It is usually identified with the saying preserved in the Gospels that the worker deserves his wages or food, given when Jesus sent out his disciples (Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10). This is one of the few places where Paul cites Jesus’s teaching directly.

verse.text: But I have made use of none of these things. And I am not writing this so that it may be done that way in my case. For I would rather die than— no one will empty my boast!

note.term: than— no one will empty my boast!
note.traditional: than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting

verse.note: In the earliest manuscripts Paul’s sentence breaks off and restarts, apparently under the pressure of feeling. Many later manuscripts smooth it into “than that anyone should make my boast empty”, and most English versions translate the smoothed sense. The broken sentence is kept here as the editors print it.

verse.text: For if I proclaim the good news, I have no boast in that, for necessity presses on me; woe to me if I do not proclaim the good news!
For if I do this by my own choice, I have a wage; but if not by my own choice, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a worker’s pay, and the whole chapter is about whether Paul may be paid for his work. “Reward” is the traditional rendering and is not wrong. “Wage” keeps the paradox of the next verse in view: Paul’s pay is to work without pay.

A steward managed a household or estate for its owner and was very often a slave, who did what he was assigned and was owed no wages for it. Paul’s point is that his preaching is a charge laid on him, not a job he chose. Some punctuate differently, running this clause into the next verse: “if not by my own choice I have been entrusted with a stewardship, what then is my wage?”

verse.text: What then is my wage? That in proclaiming the good news I may offer the good news free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the good news.
For though I am free from all, I have made myself a slave to all, so that I might win more of them.
To the Jews I became as a Jew, so that I might win Jews; to those under the law as one under the law, though I myself am not under the law, so that I might win those under the law;
to those outside the law as one outside the law, though I am not outside God’s law but inside Christ’s law, so that I might win those outside the law.
verse.note: Paul plays on two adjectives, literally “law-less” and “in-law”, each followed by a bare genitive: “not lawless of God but in-law of Christ”. The traditional “under the law of Christ” borrows the phrase “under the law” that Paul has just said does not apply to him, and blurs the contrast. The genitives could also be read as “toward God” and “toward Christ”, and what “Christ’s law” covers is debated.

verse.text: To the weak I became weak, so that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, so that by all means I might save some.
I do everything for the sake of the good news, so that I may become a partner in it.

note.traditional: share with them in its blessings

verse.note: The Greek says only “a joint partner of it”, meaning of the good news. Most translations supply “blessings”, taking Paul to mean that he hopes to share in the salvation the good news brings. Others take him to mean a partner in its work and progress, and the rendering leaves both open.

verse.text: Do you not know that the runners in a stadium all run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may seize it.
Everyone who competes exercises self-control in everything. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable one.
verse.note: Corinth oversaw the Isthmian Games, held every two years nearby and among the major athletic festivals of the Greek world. The victor’s prize was a wreath of foliage, pine or celery, which soon withered. Competitors trained under strict discipline before the games, which is the self-control Paul refers to.

verse.text: So that is how I run: not aimlessly. That is how I box: not as one beating the air.
No, I batter my body and make it my slave, so that after preaching to others I myself may not be disqualified.
verse.note: The verb literally means to strike someone under the eye, to give a black eye, and it continues the boxing image of the previous verse. Most modern translations soften it to “discipline” or “keep under control”. Paul is speaking figuratively of rigorous self-mastery, not of self-harm, but the image he uses is a boxer’s blow.

verse.text: For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, that our ancestors were all under the cloud and all passed through the sea,
and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
and all ate the same spiritual food,
and all drank the same spiritual drink, for they used to drink from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.

note.term: a spiritual rock that followed them

verse.note: Water comes from a rock at both the start and the end of the wilderness journey (Exodus 17; Numbers 20). Jewish interpretive tradition, attested around Paul's time and later, concluded that the rock or well travelled with Israel. Paul appears to assume this tradition and identifies the rock with Christ.

verse.text: But with most of them God was not pleased, for they were laid low in the wilderness.
Now these things took place as examples for us, so that we would not be people who crave evil things, as they craved.
verse.note: The Greek word means a pattern or model, and the phrase can be read as 'examples for us' (warnings to learn from) or 'types of us' (events that prefigure the later community). Most translations take the first sense, which fits the warnings that follow. The second is possible and was influential in later Christian reading of the Old Testament.

verse.text: Do not become idolaters, as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and got up to revel.”
verse.note: The quotation is Exodus 32:6, describing the feast before the golden calf. The verb covers dancing, sport and festive merrymaking, here in a setting of idol worship. 'Play' now suggests children's games, so 'revel' is used. Many translations keep 'play'.

verse.text: Nor let us commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.
verse.note: The reference is to the incident at Baal-Peor in Numbers 25, where the Hebrew and Greek texts both give twenty-four thousand dead. The reason for Paul's different figure is not known. Proposals include a slip of memory, a conflation with another census figure, or a count limited to a single day.

verse.text: Nor let us put Christ to the test, as some of them did, and were destroyed by the snakes.
verse.note: Manuscripts divide here between 'Christ', 'the Lord' and, in a few, 'God'. 'Christ' has early support and is the harder reading, since it has Israel in the wilderness testing Christ. Scribes are more likely to have softened it than to have created it, and it matches verse 4. The incident is the plague of snakes in Numbers 21.

verse.text: And do not grumble, as some of them did, and were destroyed by the destroyer.
verse.note: The word occurs only here in the New Testament. It recalls the destroying agent of God's judgment in the exodus story (Exodus 12:23) and probably refers to the plagues that followed Israel's grumbling in Numbers 14 and 16. Readers would have understood an angel sent to carry out judgment.

verse.text: Now these things were happening to them by way of example, and they were written down as a warning for us, on whom the ends of the ages have come.
So let anyone who thinks they are standing watch out that they do not fall.

No testing has overtaken you except what is common to humanity. But God is faithful: he will not let you be tested beyond what you are able, but with the testing he will also provide the way out, so that you are able to endure it.
verse.note: The Greek noun and its verb cover both an enticement to sin and a trial that proves a person; English has to choose. 'Testing' is used because Paul has just used the related verb for Israel putting Christ to the test (verse 9) and the wilderness stories are stories of trial. 'Temptation' remains the more common rendering and is not wrong; the two senses overlap here.

verse.text: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.
I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.
The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?
verse.note: The word means having a share in something together with others, or partnership. It is rendered 'sharing' here and its cognate 'sharers' in verses 18 and 20, so that the reader can see Paul using one word-family for the Lord's supper, Israel's altar and meals connected with idols. Older versions have 'communion'; many recent ones have 'participation'.

verse.text: Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
Consider Israel according to the flesh: are not those who eat the sacrifices sharers in the altar?
What am I saying, then? That food sacrificed to an idol is anything, or that an idol is anything?
No, but that what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God, and I do not want you to become sharers with demons.

note.traditional: what the Gentiles sacrifice / what pagans sacrifice

verse.note: Many manuscripts supply the subject 'the Gentiles'; the text translated here lacks it, and it is probably a scribal clarification. The sense is the same either way, since pagan worshippers are meant and not Israel from verse 18. The wording echoes Deuteronomy 32:17, 'they sacrificed to demons and not to God'.

verse.text: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? We are not stronger than he is, are we?
“All things are permitted,” but not all things are beneficial. “All things are permitted,” but not all things build up.
verse.note: Most scholars take these words, as at 6:12, to be a slogan current among the Corinthians, which Paul quotes and then qualifies; the quotation marks reflect that view. The Greek has no such marking, and the words could be Paul's own principle, restated with limits.

verse.text: Let no one seek their own good, but the other person’s.
Eat everything sold in the market without raising any question on account of conscience,
verse.note: The word is a loan from Latin for a city's provisions market, where meat and other foods were sold. Some of the meat on sale had come from animals slaughtered in temple sacrifices. A buyer would not normally know which, and that is the question Paul says need not be asked.

verse.text: for “the earth is the Lord’s, and all that fills it.”
If one of the unbelievers invites you and you want to go, eat everything set before you without raising any question on account of conscience.
But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” do not eat it, on account of the one who pointed it out and on account of conscience;
verse.note: The speaker uses the ordinary, respectful pagan term for meat from a temple sacrifice. It is not the disparaging Jewish and Christian term 'sacrificed to an idol' that Paul uses in verse 19. Whether the speaker is the pagan host, another guest or a fellow believer is not stated.

verse.text: I mean not your own conscience but the other person’s. For why should my freedom be judged by someone else’s conscience?

note.term: why should my freedom be judged

verse.note: How these two questions fit the argument is disputed. They may give Paul's reason for the general rule of verses 25 to 27, that a believer's freedom is not really subject to another's scruples even when he abstains. They may instead voice an objection from the Corinthians, or explain why one should not invite condemnation by eating. In verse 30 'with thanks' could also be rendered 'by grace'.

verse.text: If I partake with thanks, why am I denounced for something I give thanks for?
So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
Give no cause for stumbling, whether to Jews or to Greeks or to the assembly of God,
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' now suggests a building or institution, so this translation uses 'assembly' throughout. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering, and some object that 'assembly' sounds like a single meeting when an ongoing community is meant.

verse.text: just as I also try to please everyone in everything, not seeking my own benefit but that of the many, so that they may be saved.
Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.
Now I praise you because you remember me in everything and hold fast to the traditions just as I handed them on to you.
But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of a woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary word for the physical head, and Paul plays on the literal and figurative senses throughout verses 3–10. What the figure means is disputed: the majority view is that it signals authority or pre-eminence, while a substantial minority argue for 'source' or 'origin', pointing to verses 8 and 12. The translation keeps 'head' so that the wordplay stays visible and the question stays open.

Greek uses the same words for 'man' and 'husband' and for 'woman' and 'wife'. Some translations render this clause 'the head of a wife is her husband' and read the whole passage as being about married couples. The appeal to creation in verses 8–9 and 12 suits the broader 'man' and 'woman', which is used here throughout, but the narrower sense cannot be ruled out.

verse.text: Every man who prays or prophesies with something down over his head shames his head;

note.term: with something down over his head

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'having down from the head' and does not name what hangs down. Most interpreters take it as a cloth covering, such as the fold of the toga that Roman men drew over the head when offering sacrifice. Others, noting verses 14–15, take it as long hair worn loose. The rendering leaves the object unstated, as the Greek does.

verse.text: but every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered shames her head, for she is one and the same as the woman who has been shaved.
For if a woman does not cover herself, let her have her hair cut off as well; but if it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut off or to be shaved, let her cover herself.
For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man.
For man is not from woman, but woman from man;
and indeed man was not created for the sake of the woman, but woman for the sake of the man.
For this reason the woman ought to have authority over her head, because of the angels.

note.traditional: have a symbol of authority on her head

verse.note: The Greek says only 'have authority over [or on] the head'; the words 'a symbol of' are supplied by most translations, on the view that the covering is a sign of the authority she is under. Elsewhere, though, 'to have authority over' something means to exercise control over it, which would make the woman the one who holds authority over her own head. Both readings have serious scholarly support, and the plain wording of the Greek is kept here.

Paul does not explain this phrase and its meaning is uncertain. The most common suggestion is that angels were thought to be present at the community's worship and to watch over its good order, an idea found in Jewish texts of the period. Others see a reference to the angels of Genesis 6 who desired human women, or take the word in its other sense of human 'messengers' visiting from elsewhere.

verse.text: Nevertheless, in the Lord neither is woman apart from man nor man apart from woman.
For just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; and all things are from God.
Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God uncovered?
Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair, it is a dishonor to him,
but if a woman wears long hair, it is her glory? For long hair has been given as a wrap.
verse.note: The noun means a garment wrapped around the body, and is a different word from the 'cover' and 'uncovered' of verses 5–13. The preposition can mean 'as, answering to' or 'instead of'. On the second reading a woman's long hair takes the place of a garment, which some scholars use to argue that the whole passage concerns hairstyle rather than a veil. Most take it in the first sense, as an argument from nature supporting a covering.

verse.text: But if anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor do the assemblies of God.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city's citizen assembly, or, in the Greek Old Testament, Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation to keep the first-century sense.

It is not clear which custom is meant. It may be the practice Paul has been arguing against (women praying uncovered), which is why some translations paraphrase as 'no other practice'. It may instead be the custom of being contentious. The Greek word means 'such', not 'other', and is translated accordingly.

verse.text: But in giving this instruction I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse.
For in the first place, when you come together as an assembly, I hear that there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it.
For there must indeed be factions among you, so that those who stand the test may become evident among you.
So when you come together in one place, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat,
for in the eating each one goes ahead with his own supper, and one goes hungry while another gets drunk.
verse.note: At this period the Lord's supper was part of a full shared meal, usually in a wealthier member's house. The verb normally means to take or do something beforehand, suggesting that those with leisure and food began before poorer members arrived; this fits 'wait for one another' in verse 33. Some scholars argue that it means simply 'consumes', so that the fault is eating one's own food without sharing rather than eating early.

verse.text: Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the assembly of God and shame those who have nothing? What should I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.
For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was being handed over, took bread,
verse.note: Most translations have 'betrayed', referring to Judas, and that may be what is in view. But the verb is the ordinary word for handing over, the same one translated 'handed on' earlier in this verse, and Paul elsewhere uses it of God giving up his Son and of Christ giving himself up (Romans 8:32; Galatians 2:20). 'Handed over' keeps the repetition and leaves room for the wider sense.

verse.text: and after giving thanks he broke it and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read simply 'which is for you'. Later copies add 'broken' (or in a few cases 'given'), and many also add 'Take, eat' before 'This is my body'; these readings underlie the King James Version. They are generally regarded as expansions influenced by the Gospel accounts and by liturgical use.
