verse.text: In the same way he took the cup also, after the supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
So then, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be answerable for the body and the blood of the Lord.
Let a person test themselves, and so eat from the bread and drink from the cup;
for the one who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on themselves.
verse.note: 'The body' may be the body of Christ signified by the bread, or the community as Christ's body (as in 10:17 and chapter 12), which the Corinthians were dishonoring by humiliating their poorer members; many scholars think both are in play. Later manuscripts add 'unworthily' and 'of the Lord', which narrows the sense to the first. Verses 29–34 play on a single Greek root, reflected here in 'judgment', 'discerning', 'judged' and 'condemned'.

verse.text: That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep.
But if we were discerning ourselves, we would not be judged;
yet when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
So then, my brothers and sisters, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.
verse.note: Everywhere else in the New Testament this verb means 'wait for', and that is the majority rendering here. Outside the New Testament it can also mean 'receive' or 'welcome', and some scholars prefer 'welcome one another', that is, share the meal as hosts rather than merely delay it.

verse.text: If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment. The remaining matters I will set in order when I come.
Now concerning the things of the Spirit, brothers and sisters, I do not want you to be uninformed.
verse.note: The Greek is simply 'the spiritual [things or persons]'; the word 'gifts' is not there, and Paul uses a different word for 'gifts' from verse 4 on. The form could also be masculine, 'spiritual people'. Most translations supply 'gifts' from the context, which is a reasonable inference; the rendering here leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, as the Corinthian community plainly was. Some translations keep 'brothers' as more literal; many recent ones render as here.

verse.text: You know that when you were Gentiles, you were carried off to idols that cannot speak, however you happened to be led.
verse.note: This is the same Greek word translated 'nations' elsewhere; in the plural it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. Paul says 'when you were Gentiles', as though his largely non-Jewish readers no longer belong to that category. Many modern versions say 'pagans' here to bring out the religious sense.

verse.text: So I make it known to you that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says, “Jesus is accursed,” and no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit.
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word is used for something handed over to God for destruction, and so for a person under God's curse. 'Jesus is Lord' is the basic confession of the early communities. Whether anyone in Corinth actually said 'Jesus is accursed', and in what setting, is debated; Paul may be stating an extreme case to make his point.

verse.text: Now there are different allotments of gifts, but the same Spirit;
verse.note: The noun can mean either 'distribution, apportioning' or 'difference, variety', and standard lexicons allow both here. 'Allotments' is chosen because verse 11 closes the paragraph with the matching verb: the Spirit 'allotting' to each one. Most translations have 'varieties' in verses 4–6, which loses that link.

verse.text: and there are different allotments of service, and the same Lord;
and there are different allotments of workings, but the same God, who works all of them in everyone.
To each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.
For to one a word of wisdom is given through the Spirit, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit,
to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,
to another workings of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the distinguishing of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for the tongue and for a language. 'Tongues' is kept as the established term for the Spirit-prompted speech Paul discusses at length in chapter 14, but a first-century reader would simply have heard 'kinds of languages'. What kind of speech this was, and how it relates to the languages of Acts 2, is disputed.

verse.text: But one and the same Spirit works all these things, allotting to each one individually just as he determines.
For just as the body is one and has many parts, and all the parts of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.
verse.note: The word means a limb or organ of the body. 'Member' once meant exactly that, but a modern reader hears it as belonging to a club or congregation, a sense that actually derives from this passage. 'Parts' keeps the bodily picture; several modern translations do the same.

verse.text: For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink.

note.traditional: by one Spirit / in one Spirit

verse.note: The preposition can mean 'in' (the Spirit as the element in which believers are baptized) or 'by' (the Spirit as the one who baptizes). Translations are divided. 'In' matches the Gospels' phrase 'baptize in the Holy Spirit' and the image of drinking that follows; the same preposition is rendered 'by' in verses 3 and 9, where agency is the natural sense.

verse.text: For indeed the body is not one part but many.
If the foot were to say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” it would not for that reason cease to belong to the body.
And if the ear were to say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” it would not for that reason cease to belong to the body.
If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be?
But as it is, God placed the parts in the body, each one of them, just as he wished.
If they were all one part, where would the body be?
But as it is, there are many parts, yet one body.
The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”
On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are all the more necessary,
and those parts of the body that we think less honorable we clothe with greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are made all the more presentable,
while our presentable parts have no such need. But God has blended the body together, giving greater honor to the part that lacks it,
so that there may be no division in the body, but the parts may have the same concern for one another.
And if one part suffers, all the parts suffer with it; if one part is honored, all the parts rejoice with it.
Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you a part of it.
And God placed in the assembly first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, acts of assistance, acts of guidance, kinds of tongues.
verse.note: The Greek word was the everyday term for a civic gathering and the Greek Old Testament's word for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' throughout so that the reader can see it is one word.

The word is literally the steering of a ship; in the Greek book of Proverbs it is used for wise direction or counsel. It occurs only here in the New Testament. Whether Paul means leadership of the community or the giving of sound guidance more generally is uncertain; translations vary between 'administration', 'leadership' and 'guidance'.

verse.text: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles?
Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?
But be eager for the greater gifts. And further, I will show you a way beyond comparison.
verse.note: The Greek form can be a command ('be eager for') or a statement ('you are eager for'). Most translations take it as a command, as in 14:1, where the same verb is clearly an instruction. A minority read it as a mild rebuke: 'you are eager for the greater gifts, but I will show you a better way.'

verse.text: If I speak in the tongues of people and of angels but do not have love, I have become resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a language as well as for the organ of speech; a first-century reader would have heard ‘the languages of people and of angels’. The traditional ‘tongues’ is kept because it is the established name for the gift of speech discussed in chapters 12 to 14.

The Greek names the metal, not an instrument, and literally says ‘echoing bronze’. Most modern versions take it as a gong. Some scholars think it refers to the bronze resonating vessels used to amplify sound in theatres, which make noise but say nothing. The reference is uncertain, so the rendering stays with what the Greek states.

verse.text: And if I have the gift of prophecy and understand all the mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.
And if I dole out all my possessions as food, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have love, I gain nothing.
verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between two verbs that differ by a single letter: ‘so that I may be burned’ and ‘so that I may boast’. The SBL text translated here reads ‘be burned’. Several of the earliest manuscripts read ‘boast’, which the Nestle-Aland edition and a number of recent translations adopt. Scholars remain divided.

verse.text: Love is patient, love is kind; love does not envy, does not brag, is not puffed up,
does not behave shamefully, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, does not keep count of wrongs,
verse.note: The verb means to act in a way that is disgraceful or indecent by the standards of an honour-conscious society, which is stronger than bad manners. Paul uses the same word group for dishonourable conduct elsewhere in this letter. ‘Is not rude’ is the common modern rendering and is not wrong, only weaker.

note.term: does not keep count of wrongs
note.traditional: thinks no evil; keeps no record of wrongs

verse.note: The verb is a bookkeeping term, to reckon or enter in an account, and the object is literally ‘the evil’. Most scholars take this to mean that love does not keep a tally of injuries done to it. The phrase can also mean ‘does not plot evil’, a sense it has in the Greek Old Testament, and older versions rendered it ‘thinks no evil’.

verse.text: does not rejoice over wrongdoing but rejoices together with the truth;
it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
verse.note: The verb can mean either ‘endure, put up with’ or ‘cover, keep confidential’, so the clause may say that love covers everything in silence and does not expose others’ faults. ‘Bears’ follows Paul’s use of the verb elsewhere for enduring hardship. The fourfold ‘all things’ may also be adverbial, ‘in everything’ or ‘always’, which avoids the suggestion that love is gullible.

verse.text: Love never falls. But as for prophecies, they will be done away with; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will be done away with.

note.traditional: Love never fails; Love never ends

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for falling, used figuratively of something collapsing or ceasing to stand. ‘Never fails’ can suggest to a modern reader that love always succeeds. The point is that love, unlike prophecy, tongues and knowledge, never comes to an end.

note.term: they will be done away with
note.traditional: will fail / vanish away / pass away; put away (v. 11)

verse.note: Paul uses the same verb four times in verses 8 to 11: of prophecies, of knowledge, of what is partial, and of an adult leaving childish ways behind. It means to bring to an end or put out of use. Many translations vary the English; one rendering is used here throughout so that the repetition can be heard.

verse.text: For we know in part and we prophesy in part;
but when what is complete comes, what is in part will be done away with.

note.traditional: that which is perfect; the perfect

verse.note: The adjective means complete, whole or fully grown, and here it stands opposite ‘what is in part’. ‘Complete’ therefore states the contrast more exactly than ‘perfect’, which suggests moral flawlessness. Most scholars take the reference to be the consummation at Christ’s return, when partial knowledge gives way to seeing ‘face to face’ (verse 12).

verse.text: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child; when I became a man, I did away with the things of a child.
For now we see by means of a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, just as I have also been fully known.

note.term: by means of a mirror, in a riddle
note.traditional: through a glass, darkly; in a mirror dimly

verse.note: The Greek says literally ‘through a mirror, in a riddle’. Ancient mirrors were polished metal, and the point is probably that one sees only a reflection and not the thing itself. ‘In a riddle’ echoes Numbers 12:8 in the Greek Old Testament, where God speaks with Moses mouth to mouth and ‘not through riddles’. ‘Dimly’ and ‘darkly’ are interpretive paraphrases of that phrase.

verse.text: And now faith, hope, love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love.
verse.note: The opening words can be temporal (‘in the present time’) or logical (‘as things stand’, ‘in fact’). On the first reading faith and hope belong to the present age and love alone lasts beyond it. On the second all three remain, in contrast to the gifts that pass away, and love is still the greatest. Interpreters are divided.

verse.text: Pursue love, and be eager for the spiritual gifts, but even more that you may prophesy.
For the one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to people but to God; for no one understands, but in the Spirit such a person speaks mysteries.
verse.note: The Greek word means both the tongue as an organ and a language, and Paul plays on both senses (see verse 9). ‘Tongue’ is kept because English can still carry both. Whether Paul has in mind human languages unknown to the speaker or speech of no human kind is debated; the chapter assumes only that hearers cannot understand it without interpretation.

note.traditional: in the Spirit / in his spirit

verse.note: The Greek has simply ‘in spirit’, without an article, and could mean God's Spirit or the speaker's own spirit, as in verses 14–16, where Paul sets ‘my spirit’ against ‘my mind’. Translations are divided. The reference to God's Spirit is chosen here because Paul has just described tongues as a gift the Spirit gives (12:10), but the other reading is equally possible.

verse.text: But the one who prophesies speaks to people for building up and encouragement and comfort.
Whoever speaks in a tongue builds themselves up, but whoever prophesies builds up the assembly.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘church’, which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas ‘church’ now suggests a building or an institution. In this chapter the sense of people actually gathered in one place is especially prominent.

verse.text: I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more that you may prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless that person interprets, so that the assembly may receive building up.
Now, brothers and sisters, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I speak to you by revelation or by knowledge or by prophecy or by teaching?
Even with lifeless things that give a sound, whether pipe or lyre: if they give no distinction to the notes, how will it be known what is being played on the pipe or the lyre?
verse.note: Many translations have ‘flute’ and ‘harp’. The aulos was a reed-blown pipe, closer to an oboe than to a modern flute, and the kithara was a large lyre rather than a harp. They were the standard wind and string instruments of Greek public life.

verse.text: And indeed, if the trumpet gives an unclear sound, who will get ready for battle?
So also with you: if with the tongue you do not give intelligible speech, how will it be known what is being said? For you will be speaking into the air.
There are, it may be, so many kinds of languages in the world, and none is without meaning.
So if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the one speaking, and the one speaking a foreigner to me.
So also with you: since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, seek to abound for the building up of the assembly.
verse.note: The Greek says literally that the Corinthians are ‘eager for spirits’. Most interpreters take this as shorthand for the Spirit's gifts or workings, and the rendering follows that view because ‘spirits’ alone would mislead. A minority think Paul is echoing the Corinthians' own way of speaking about inspiring spirits. The same plural recurs in verse 32, ‘the spirits of prophets’.

verse.text: Therefore the one who speaks in a tongue should pray to be able to interpret.
For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.
What then? I will pray with my spirit, and I will pray with my mind also; I will sing with my spirit, and I will sing with my mind also.
Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninstructed say the Amen to your thanksgiving, since that person does not know what you are saying?
verse.note: The word denotes a layperson or non-expert, someone without the relevant training or skill (compare Acts 4:13; 2 Corinthians 11:6). Here it may mean any worshipper who does not understand the tongue being spoken, or a distinct group of interested outsiders who are not yet full members; verses 23–24 set such people alongside unbelievers. Translations vary among ‘outsider’, ‘inquirer’, ‘unlearned’ and ‘ungifted’.

verse.text: For you are giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not built up.
I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you;
but in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my mind, so that I may instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
Brothers and sisters, do not be children in your thinking; in evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.
In the Law it is written: “By people of other tongues and by the lips of others I will speak to this people, and not even so will they listen to me, says the Lord.”
verse.note: ‘The Law’ here means Scripture as a whole, not only the five books of Moses. The quotation is from Isaiah 28:11–12, where God warns that Israel, having refused plain speech, will hear him through the foreign language of invaders. Paul's wording matches neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint closely.

verse.text: So then, tongues are for a sign not to those who believe but to unbelievers, while prophecy is not for unbelievers but for those who believe.
So if the whole assembly comes together in one place and all speak in tongues, and uninstructed people or unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds?
But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in, that person is convicted by all, examined by all,
the secrets of their heart come to light, and so, falling facedown, they will worship God, declaring, “God is truly among you!”
What then, brothers and sisters? When you come together, each one has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation. Let everything be done for building up.
If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be two or at most three, and one at a time, and let one person interpret.
But if there is no interpreter, let each of them keep silent in the assembly and speak to themselves and to God.
Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said.
But if a revelation comes to another who is seated, let the first keep silent.
For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged
(and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets,
for God is not a God of disorder but of peace), as in all the assemblies of the holy ones.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘saints’, which many translations keep; others use ‘God's people’. ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, whereas the word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel.

note.term: as in all the assemblies of the holy ones

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had little or no punctuation, and this clause can close the preceding sentence, as here and in the SBLGNT, or open the next: ‘As in all the assemblies of the holy ones, let the women keep silent.’ Many modern translations take the second option. The first avoids the awkward repetition ‘in all the assemblies ... in the assemblies’, though it leaves the clause trailing loosely after the parenthesis.

verse.text: Let the women keep silent in the assemblies, for they are not permitted to speak; rather, let them be subject, as the Law also says.

note.term: Let the women keep silent in the assemblies

verse.note: A few manuscripts of the Western tradition place verses 34–35 after verse 40. Some scholars conclude from this that the two verses began as a marginal comment and are not Paul's; others point out that no surviving manuscript omits them. The SBLGNT prints them here without brackets.

The Greek word means both ‘women’ and ‘wives’, and verse 35 (‘their own husbands’) suggests that married women are in view. Since Paul assumes in 11:5 that women pray and prophesy in the gathering, most interpreters take the silence required here to be limited in some way rather than absolute, though how is disputed. Which passage of ‘the Law’ is meant is also uncertain; Genesis 3:16 is often suggested.

verse.text: If they want to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in the assembly.
Or was it from you that the word of God went out? Or are you the only ones it has reached?
If anyone thinks they are a prophet or a spiritual person, they should recognize that what I am writing to you is the Lord's.

note.traditional: is a command of the Lord

verse.note: The SBLGNT reads simply ‘is the Lord's’. Most manuscripts, and most translations, read ‘is a command of the Lord’ or ‘are commands of the Lord’. The shorter reading has limited manuscript support, but the variation among the longer forms suggests that the word was added to complete the sense.

verse.text: But if anyone does not recognize this, they are not recognized.

note.traditional: let him be ignorant / he is not recognized

verse.note: Paul echoes verse 37: whoever does not recognize this is not recognized, probably by God, possibly by the community. Many later manuscripts have an imperative instead, ‘let him be ignorant’, which the King James Version follows. The verb can also mean ‘ignore’, giving ‘if anyone ignores this, he is ignored’.

verse.text: So then, my brothers and sisters, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues;
but let everything be done decently and in order.
Now I make known to you, brothers and sisters, the good news that I announced to you, which you also received, in which you also stand,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community. 'Brothers' alone now suggests to an English reader that only men are meant. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep 'brothers' and explain it in a footnote.

The Greek noun was an everyday word for good news, often the public announcement of a victory or a ruler's accession, and the verb beside it ('announced') comes from the same root. 'Gospel' has become a purely religious term in English and hides that ordinary sense. Both renderings are common in modern translations.

verse.text: through which you are also being saved, if you hold fast to the very terms in which I announced it to you—unless you believed in vain.
For I handed on to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures,

note.traditional: first of all / as of first importance

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'among the first things', which can mean first in importance or first in time (the first things Paul taught at Corinth). Most interpreters take it as importance. 'Handed on' and 'received' are the standard terms for passing on a fixed tradition, and verses 3–5 are widely regarded as a summary formula older than the letter itself.

verse.text: and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures,
and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve.
After that he appeared to more than five hundred brothers and sisters at one time, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep.
After that he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.
Last of all, as though to a miscarried child, he appeared also to me.

note.traditional: one untimely born / one born out of due time

verse.note: The Greek word means a miscarriage or stillbirth, and in the Septuagint it is an image of something wretched and lifeless. The traditional rendering softens it and suggests only that Paul came late. Why Paul uses so harsh a word of himself is debated; it may be a term of abuse used by his opponents, or a picture of his unfitness as a former persecutor.

verse.text: For I am the least of the apostles, not fit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people, used for a city's citizen assembly and in the Greek Old Testament for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: But by God's grace I am what I am, and his grace toward me did not prove empty; on the contrary, I labored harder than all of them—yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me.
So whether it was I or they, this is what we proclaim and this is what you believed.
Now if Christ is proclaimed as having been raised from the dead, how can some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?
But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then neither has Christ been raised;
and if Christ has not been raised, then our proclamation is empty, and your faith is empty too.
We are also found to be false witnesses about God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if in fact the dead are not raised.
For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised;
and if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins.
Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.
If it is only in this life that we have hoped in Christ, we are more to be pitied than all people.
But as it is, Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
verse.note: In Israel's law the first portion of the harvest was offered to God, and it stood for the whole crop still to come. Paul's point is that Christ's resurrection is not an isolated event but the beginning and guarantee of the general resurrection.

verse.text: For since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead also comes through a human being.
For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.
But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming;
verse.note: The Greek word means arrival or presence. It was regularly used for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city, and a first-century reader would probably have heard that association when it was applied to Christ.

verse.text: then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every rule and every authority and power.
verse.note: The verb means to make something inoperative, to strip it of force or bring it to an end; it is not the usual word for destroying. 'Abolish' fits both the powers of this verse and death in verse 26, where the same verb recurs. Many translations use 'destroy' in both places.

verse.text: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.
The last enemy to be abolished is death,
for “he has subjected all things under his feet.” But when it says that all things have been subjected, it is clear that this excludes the one who subjected all things to him.
And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.
Otherwise, what will those people do who are baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are they baptized on their behalf?

note.term: baptized on behalf of the dead

verse.note: The plain sense of the Greek is that some people were undergoing baptism on behalf of people who had died, and most scholars read it that way, though nothing more is known of the practice. Many other explanations have been proposed, such as baptism 'because of' the witness of dead believers. Paul refers to the practice as an argument without commending or condemning it.

verse.text: And why are we ourselves in danger every hour?
Every day I die—I swear it by my boasting in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.
If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus on merely human terms, what do I gain? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
verse.note: The verb is the term for fighting animals in the arena. Most scholars take it figuratively, of violent human opposition in Ephesus, since a Roman citizen would not normally be sent to the beasts and Paul survived; a literal reading is possible but less likely. The words that close the verse quote Isaiah 22:13.

verse.text: Do not be deceived: “Bad company corrupts good character.”
verse.note: This is a line of Greek verse, usually attributed to the comic playwright Menander, which had probably become a common proverb. Paul quotes it as a saying his readers would recognise, not as Scripture.

verse.text: Sober up as you rightly should, and stop sinning; for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to shame you.
But someone will say, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?”
Fool! What you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies.
And as for what you sow, you do not sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of something else.
But God gives it a body just as he wished, and to each of the seeds its own body.
Not all flesh is the same flesh: there is one flesh of humans, another flesh of livestock, another flesh of birds, and another of fish.
There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and that of the earthly of another.
There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; indeed, star differs from star in glory.
So it is with the resurrection of the dead. It is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable.
It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual one.
verse.note: The Greek adjective is formed from psychē, the word rendered 'living being' in the quotation in verse 45 (traditionally 'living soul'), so it describes a body animated by ordinary life as Adam's was. 'Spiritual' correspondingly describes a body animated by the Spirit, not one made of something immaterial. Some translations use 'physical' here, which most scholars think misleadingly suggests a contrast between material and non-material.

verse.text: So also it is written: “The first human, Adam, became a living being.” The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.
But the spiritual is not first; rather the natural, and then the spiritual.
The first human was from the earth, made of dust; the second human is from heaven.
As was the one made of dust, so also are those made of dust; and as is the heavenly one, so also are those who are heavenly.
And just as we have borne the image of the one made of dust, we will also bear the image of the heavenly one.
verse.note: Many early and important manuscripts read 'let us also bear', an exhortation, which differs by a single letter in Greek. The edition translated here reads the future, as do most English versions, because it suits the argument of the passage. The choice is disputed among textual scholars.

verse.text: What I am saying, brothers and sisters, is this: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.
Look, I am telling you a mystery: we will not all fall asleep, but we will all be changed,
in a moment, in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed.
For this perishable body must put on imperishability, and this mortal body must put on immortality.
And when this perishable body has put on imperishability and this mortal body has put on immortality, then the word that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.

text.q: Where, death, is your victory? Where, death, is your sting?”

verse.text: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
So then, my beloved brothers and sisters, be steadfast, immovable, always overflowing in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not empty in the Lord.
Now about the collection for the holy ones: you too should do as I directed the assemblies of Galatia.
verse.note: The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense here. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'. Here it refers specifically to the believers in Jerusalem, for whom the collection was being gathered.

A first-century hearer knew this word as the term for a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and is clear in reference, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: On the first day of every week, each of you should put something aside at home and save it up, in proportion to how you have prospered, so that no collections have to be made when I come.

note.term: On the first day of every week

verse.note: The Greek follows the Jewish way of counting days from the Sabbath, literally 'on day one of the sabbath-week', which is Sunday. The instruction is for each person to set money aside privately ('at home' is literally 'with himself'). Whether the choice of day reflects a weekly gathering of the community on Sunday is plausible but not stated.

verse.text: And when I arrive, I will send whomever you approve, with letters, to carry your gift to Jerusalem.
verse.note: The Greek phrase 'by means of letters' can attach to either verb. Most modern translations take it as here: Paul will send the approved delegates with letters of introduction. The alternative, found in some older versions, is that the Corinthians approve their delegates by letter ('whomever you approve by your letters').

This is the same Greek word translated 'grace' in verse 23. It covers favor, generosity and the concrete gift that expresses them. Paul uses it repeatedly for the Jerusalem collection, especially in 2 Corinthians 8–9.

verse.text: If it seems worthwhile for me to go as well, they will travel with me.
I will come to you after I pass through Macedonia—for I am passing through Macedonia—
and perhaps I will stay with you for a while, or even spend the winter, so that you can send me on my way wherever I go next.
For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to stay with you for some time, if the Lord permits.
But I will stay on in Ephesus until Pentecost,
for a great door for effective work has opened to me, and the opponents are many.
If Timothy comes, see that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the Lord’s work just as I am.
So let no one look down on him. Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.
Now about our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers, but he was not at all willing to come now. He will come when he has the opportunity.

note.term: he was not at all willing

verse.note: The Greek says literally 'it was not at all will that he come now', without saying whose will. Most translations take it as Apollos's own unwillingness, as here. Some interpreters understand it as God's will, since the word used absolutely can carry that sense. The following clause, 'he will come when he has the opportunity', slightly favors the first reading.

verse.text: Stay alert, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong.
verse.note: The verb is formed from the word for 'man', and older versions render it 'quit you like men' or 'act like men'. In the Septuagint it is the standard exhortation to courage, usually paired with 'be strong' as it is here (for example, in the charge to Joshua). It is addressed to the whole community, and the point is bravery and not maleness. Several modern translations render it this way.

verse.text: Let everything you do be done in love.
I urge you, brothers and sisters—you know the household of Stephanas, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia and have placed themselves at the service of the holy ones—
verse.note: The Greek masculine plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members, and the Corinthian community plainly included women. Where the whole community is meant, this translation uses 'brothers and sisters', as several modern versions do. In verses 11 and 12, where specific travelling companions are meant, 'the brothers' is kept.

verse.text: to place yourselves in turn under people like these, and under everyone who shares in the work and labors at it.
verse.note: Paul plays on two related verbs: Stephanas's household have 'placed themselves' at the service of others (verse 15), and the Corinthians are to 'place themselves under' such people. The traditional 'submit' or 'be subject' is accurate in sense but loses the echo. The call is to voluntary deference toward those who do the work, not to a formal chain of command.

verse.text: I rejoice at the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence,
for they have refreshed my spirit and yours. So give recognition to people like these.
The assemblies of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the assembly that meets in their house.
verse.note: This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of what is now Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city. It is not the continent. Paul is writing from Ephesus (verse 8).

verse.text: All the brothers and sisters greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s.
verse.note: Letters were normally dictated to a scribe. At this point Paul takes the pen and writes the closing lines himself, which served as a personal touch and as a mark of authenticity. He does the same at the end of several other letters.

verse.text: If anyone does not love the Lord, let that person be accursed. Our Lord, come!
verse.note: Paul writes an Aramaic phrase in Greek letters without translating it, which suggests it was a fixed prayer inherited from the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers. Divided as marana tha, as in the Greek text followed here, it is a prayer: 'Our Lord, come!' Divided as maran atha it would be a statement: 'Our Lord has come' or 'is coming'. Most scholars prefer the prayer, in part because Revelation 22:20 has a similar prayer in Greek. Older versions leave the Aramaic untranslated.

verse.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.
My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus.
